metadata.title: A Generalization of Brouwer's Fixed Point Theorem
metadata.source_note: Extracted from PDF->text fallback; .tex source not available. Math fidelity reduced.

nodes.name: Brouwer's Fixed Point Theorem
nodes.statement: If $x \mapsto \varphi(x)$ is a continuous point-to-point mapping of an $r$-dimensional closed simplex $S$ into itself, then there exists $x_0 \in S$ such that $x_0 = \varphi(x_0)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Every continuous self-map of a closed simplex has a fixed point.
assumptions: $\varphi: S \to S$ is a continuous point-to-point mapping

nodes.name: Upper semi-continuous point-to-set mapping
nodes.statement: A point-to-set mapping $x \mapsto \Phi(x) \in \mathfrak{F}(S)$ of $S$ into the family $\mathfrak{F}(S)$ of all closed convex subsets of $S$ is called upper semi-continuous if $x_n \to x_0$, $y_n \in \Phi(x_n)$, and $y_n \to y_0$ imply $y_0 \in \Phi(x_0)$.
nodes.statement_clean: A set-valued map is upper semi-continuous if its graph is closed.
nodes.notes: The text remarks this condition is equivalent to the graph $\{(x, y) : y \in \Phi(x)\} \subset S \times S$ being closed.

nodes.name: Kakutani's Fixed Point Theorem (simplex form)
nodes.statement: If $x \mapsto \Phi(x)$ is an upper semi-continuous point-to-set mapping of an $r$-dimensional closed simplex $S$ into $\mathfrak{F}(S)$, then there exists $x_0 \in S$ such that $x_0 \in \Phi(x_0)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Every upper semi-continuous closed-convex-valued self-map of a closed simplex has a fixed point.
assumptions: $\Phi: S \to \mathfrak{F}(S)$ assigns to each $x \in S$ a closed convex subset of $S$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Apply Brouwer's theorem to a piecewise-linear selection on the $n$-th barycentric subdivision; pass to a convergent subsequence and use upper semi-continuity together with convexity of $\Phi(x_0)$ to conclude $x_0 \in \Phi(x_0)$.

nodes.name: Construct piecewise-linear selection on barycentric subdivision
nodes.statement: Let $S^{(n)}$ be the $n$-th barycentric simplicial subdivision of $S$. For each vertex $x_n$ of $S^{(n)}$ pick an arbitrary $y_n \in \Phi(x_n)$, and extend linearly inside each simplex to obtain a continuous map $x \mapsto \varphi_n(x)$ of $S$ into itself.

nodes.name: Apply Brouwer's theorem to obtain approximate fixed points
nodes.statement: By Brouwer's fixed point theorem, for each $n$ there exists $x^{(n)} \in S$ with $x^{(n)} = \varphi_n(x^{(n)})$.

nodes.name: Extract convergent subsequence
nodes.statement: Take a subsequence $\{x^{(n_k)}\}$ converging to a point $x_0 \in S$. Let $\Delta_{n_k}$ be an $r$-simplex of $S^{(n_k)}$ containing $x^{(n_k)}$ with vertices $x_{n_k}^0, \dots, x_{n_k}^r$, so each $x_{n_k}^i \to x_0$ and $x^{(n_k)} = \sum_{i=0}^{r} \lambda_{n_k}^i x_{n_k}^i$ with $\lambda_{n_k}^i \geq 0$ and $\sum_i \lambda_{n_k}^i = 1$.

nodes.name: Pass to limit using upper semi-continuity
nodes.statement: Setting $y_{n_k}^i = \varphi_{n_k}(x_{n_k}^i) \in \Phi(x_{n_k}^i)$ and refining further so that $y_{n_k}^i \to y^i$ and $\lambda_{n_k}^i \to \lambda^i$, upper semi-continuity gives $y^i \in \Phi(x_0)$ for each $i$.

nodes.name: Conclude via convexity of $\Phi(x_0)$
nodes.statement: Since $x_0 = \sum_i \lambda^i y^i$ and each $y^i \in \Phi(x_0)$, convexity of $\Phi(x_0)$ yields $x_0 \in \Phi(x_0)$.

nodes.name: Brouwer as a special case
nodes.statement: Brouwer's fixed point theorem is the special case of Theorem 1 in which each $\Phi(x)$ consists of a single point $\varphi(x)$; upper semi-continuity then reduces to continuity of $\varphi$.

nodes.name: Kakutani's Fixed Point Theorem (convex set form)
nodes.statement: Theorem 1 remains valid if $S$ is replaced by an arbitrary bounded closed convex set in a Euclidean space.
nodes.statement_clean: The fixed point theorem extends from simplices to all bounded closed convex sets.
assumptions: $S$ is a bounded closed convex set in a Euclidean space
$\Phi: S \to \mathfrak{F}(S)$ is upper semi-continuous and closed-convex-valued

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary
nodes.statement: Embed $S$ into a containing simplex $S'$, take a continuous retraction $\psi: S' \to S$, apply Theorem 1 to $\Phi \circ \psi$ on $S'$, and use the retracting property to obtain a fixed point in $S$.

nodes.name: Common point of two convex-fibered closed sets (von Neumann)
nodes.statement: Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ and $L \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be bounded closed convex sets. Let $U, V \subset K \times L$ be closed and such that for every $x_0 \in K$ the slice $U_{x_0} = \{y \in L : (x_0, y) \in U\}$ is non-empty, closed and convex, and for every $y_0 \in L$ the slice $V_{y_0} = \{x \in K : (x, y_0) \in V\}$ is non-empty, closed and convex. Then $U \cap V \neq \emptyset$.
nodes.statement_clean: Two closed sets with non-empty closed convex fibers in both directions intersect.
assumptions: For every $x_0 \in K$, $U_{x_0}$ is non-empty, closed and convex
For every $y_0 \in L$, $V_{y_0}$ is non-empty, closed and convex
nodes.notes: The result is attributed to von Neumann (1937); Kakutani's contribution here is the simpler proof via the corollary of Theorem 1.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Define $\Phi(z) = V_y \times U_x$ on $S = K \times L$ for $z = (x, y)$; this map is upper semi-continuous and closed-convex-valued, so the corollary of Theorem 1 yields a fixed point $z_0 \in \Phi(z_0)$, equivalent to $z_0 \in U \cap V$.

nodes.name: Minimax theorem (von Neumann)
nodes.statement: Let $f(x, y)$ be a continuous real-valued function on $K \times L$, where $K, L$ are bounded closed convex sets in Euclidean spaces. Suppose for every $x_0 \in K$ and every $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ the set $\{y \in L : f(x_0, y) \leq \alpha\}$ is convex, and for every $y_0 \in L$ and every $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ the set $\{x \in K : f(x, y_0) \geq \beta\}$ is convex. Then $\max_{x \in K} \min_{y \in L} f(x, y) = \min_{y \in L} \max_{x \in K} f(x, y)$.
nodes.statement_clean: Under suitable convexity, max-min equals min-max for continuous payoff functions.
assumptions: For each $x_0, \alpha$: $\{y : f(x_0, y) \leq \alpha\}$ is convex (quasi-convexity in $y$)
For each $y_0, \beta$: $\{x : f(x, y_0) \geq \beta\}$ is convex (quasi-concavity in $x$)
conclusions: $\max_{x \in K} \min_{y \in L} f(x, y) = \min_{y \in L} \max_{x \in K} f(x, y)$
nodes.notes: The remark identifies this as a fundamental theorem of von Neumann's game theory; Kakutani's contribution is the proof via Theorem 2.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Let $U = \{(x_0, y_0) : f(x_0, y_0) = \min_{y \in L} f(x_0, y)\}$ and $V = \{(x_0, y_0) : f(x_0, y_0) = \max_{x \in K} f(x, y_0)\}$. The convexity hypotheses make these sets satisfy Theorem 2, yielding $(x_0, y_0)$ with $f(x_0, y_0) = \min_y f(x_0, y) = \max_x f(x, y_0)$, which sandwiches $\min_y \max_x f$ and $\max_x \min_y f$ together.

nodes.name: Game-theoretic significance
nodes.statement: Theorem 3 is one of the fundamental theorems in the theory of games developed by J. von Neumann, and Theorem 2 has applications to mathematical economics.
